answer.question: What should I consider when replacing an older Northglenn lawn?
answer.answer: Show us tree roots, settled areas and any original irrigation you want to remove or retain. Keep walking routes and the patio in the plan. A lawn, pet area or short putting green can then be compared against the space and care routine you want.

blocks.h2: Make the square yard do more than one job.
paras: A pet area along the route from the door can be separate from seating or a small green. Leave clear walking space and planting that you want to keep. Under established trees, discuss roots and debris cleanup before deciding the turf boundary.
For putting, choose the distances that fit and where you will stand. Extra cups are not useful if they leave no comfortable route around the surface.

blocks.h2: Use Northglenn’s information for your property.
paras: Do not assume a nearby Thornton turf program applies to a Northglenn address. Confirm your provider and any incentive eligibility directly before including it in the budget.

Check the City and any applicable property requirements for the actual work. The absence of an association does not settle front-yard, grading or drainage questions. Ask for preparation and any unresolved site conditions to be stated in the estimate.

blocks.h2: A planned 1960s suburb, mostly built before HOAs.
paras: Northglenn began in 1959 as a master-planned community by developer Jordon Perlmutter and incorporated on 19 April 1969 (Wikipedia). More of its housing went up in the 1960s than in any other decade, the median home dates from 1974, and its north end was never redeveloped.

The typical house is an original ranch or split-level with a small, square back yard, a carport or a single detached garage, and big trees. Because those streets predate the HOA era, many have no design committee at all: no approval packet, just a layout you approve and a start date.

Where a street does have an HOA, state law says its design guidelines can't rule out nonvegetative turf behind a detached house (SB23-178). The city is the one with turf rules in writing. Its development code gives artificial turf a subsection of its own, 11-4-7(f), which requires a green colour similar to natural grass and rules out indoor or outdoor carpeting in its place, and the materials list that applies to an existing single-family yard points straight at it (Northglenn Municipal Code).
Front yards are where to be careful. Ask Planning and Development how 11-4-7 reads on your lot and whether the work needs a permit, and bring the answer to the visit.

blocks.h2: Two watering days, and your house number picks them.
paras: Northglenn supplies and bills its own water, so its rules are its own. The City Council declared a Stage 2 drought on 13 April 2026, 8 votes to none (City of Northglenn), after Standley Lake, the city's storage, failed to fill. Mandatory restrictions came with it, and which two days you water depends on your address: even numbers Sunday and Thursday, odd numbers Wednesday and Saturday, apartments, businesses and HOA common areas Tuesday and Friday, none of it between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. (CR-67).

Those days cost money too. Past 18,000 gallons in a month a home's bill picks up the Stage 2 surcharge of $2.00 per thousand gallons (Northglenn Municipal Code), and on 13 April the Council also adopted a schedule of warnings and fines for breaking the restrictions: an educational door hanger, then $50, $300 and $999, assessed through the city utility bill (CR-68).

That is the schedule a fifty-year-old bluegrass lawn now lives on, under trees that were already taking most of the water. Turf needs none of those days, and the shade that beat the lawn keeps it cooler on a hot afternoon (more on turf and heat). The declaration stays in effect until the city lifts it, and the city manager can lift it without another vote, so ask Northglenn Public Works for the current stage before you plan around it.

blocks.h2: Loam over shale, not the metro's worst clay.
paras: USDA soil data for Northglenn shows Platner loam, about 19% clay on 3 to 5% slopes, along with Ulm at 23.5% clay and Renohill at 23%, and Shingle and Apishapa in smaller patches (USDA). Shrink-swell runs low to moderate, so swelling clay isn't the Northglenn story.
Renohill is shallow to shale, which can limit how deep a dig goes in places. The free visit shows how deep we can go, and the packed soil is prepared before any base goes in.

The fall of the ground matters more here than the clay does. The city's code bars artificial turf on slopes greater than six percent (Northglenn Municipal Code), which is a grade you measure rather than eyeball, so we take the fall of the yard at the free visit instead of assuming it. The same section sets how the surface goes down: sod off first, compacted porous road base under it, edges and seams anchored, and no sewn seams.

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Northglenn, CO?
faq.a: We install artificial turf, pet turf and backyard putting greens in Northglenn, CO. Northglenn was planned from 1959, and more of it went up in the 1960s than in any other decade, so many yards share a profile: small, square and shaded by trees that have beaten the bluegrass, on streets that often predate HOAs. The city supplies its own water, and under the Stage 2 drought it declared in April 2026 your lawn gets two watering days a week, set by your house number. Call 303-349-2368 for a free estimate.

faq.q: Do I need HOA approval for turf in Northglenn?
faq.a: Often not. Much of Northglenn was built in the 1960s and '70s, before HOAs were standard, so many streets have no association. If yours does, SB23-178 lets it set design rules for back-yard turf on a detached home, but not ban it (SB23-178).

faq.q: Does Thornton's turf rebate apply in Northglenn?
faq.a: No. That rebate is a Thornton Water program for its own customers, with its own permit step (Thornton Water), and Northglenn supplies and bills its own water. The conservation help Northglenn listed with its Stage 2 drought is lawn replacement, Garden in a Box, Slow the Flow irrigation checkups and fixture rebates (City of Northglenn). None of it is an artificial turf rebate, so ask Northglenn Public Works before you count on one.

faq.q: Can turf go on a slope in Northglenn?
faq.a: Only a gentle one. The city's code says artificial turf shall not be installed on slopes greater than six percent, and that it has to be a green colour similar to natural grass, with indoor or outdoor carpeting ruled out in its place (Northglenn Municipal Code). Where a yard runs steeper, the grade has to be cut to suit before any base goes in, which is a decision for the visit.

faq.q: Is there a golf course in Northglenn?
faq.a: No, there's no municipal or private course inside the city. The nearest are Thorncreek in Thornton, and Legacy Ridge and Walnut Creek in Westminster, which is one good reason for a green in the back yard.

Mostly loam: Platner, Ulm and Renohill soils of roughly 19 to 23.5% clay, with low to moderate shrink-swell (USDA). The bigger problem is fifty years of compaction and tree roots, which the site prep deals with.
